prize_parts.citation: For constructing population-scale administrative-data measures of intergenerational mobility, and for design-based evidence on how childhood exposure to place shapes later economic opportunity.

statement.case_for: My laureates and preferred part are unchanged from round 1. The citation is narrower and my reasoning is revised. B002 gave economists a new empirical object: intergenerational mobility measured by place on linked administrative records, together with designs such as movers and childhood-exposure comparisons that separate causal place effects from sorting. The measurement standard and the designs travel to other countries' registers, so they should survive even if particular point estimates move. That is the part I would reward. The shorter citation deliberately claims less than my round-1 wording: it credits measurement and exposure-based designs, and does not endorse long-run causal place-effect conclusions or specific policy prescriptions. Under one common weighting of identification quality, conceptual originality, maturity and attribution tractability, my reading is as follows. B002 is strongest on identification and checkability, moderate on conceptual novelty and on maturity, and good on attribution apart from the Katz question. B004 as a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is stronger on maturity and originality, weaker on direct identification, and clean on attribution. B027 is strongest on maturity, with weaker identification. B015 has the longest record but the most contestable credit. The margin between B002 and a B004 pair is narrow. A committee that weights maturity most heavily could sensibly rank the B004 pair first, and I say so openly. I put B002 first because direct testability of its claims and the clarity of its trio outweigh the shorter record for me. I do not use opening support counts as evidence of merit, and the chair's observation that no configuration reaches six votes does not move me toward any configuration for the sake of agreement.
statement.case_against: There are three main reservations, and one of them is a correction to my own round-1 argument. First, maturity: the core results date from about 2014 to 2022, and the long-run causal reading of place effects is still contested. Second, attribution: from general knowledge, which I have not verified here, the reanalysis of Moving to Opportunity that made it a statement about childhood exposure was by Chetty, Hendren and Katz. My round-1 reply to Hjalmarsson and others said that reanalysis was done by the Chetty-Hendren-Friedman group, and that was wrong. It strengthens Katz's claim on the exposure-effects half of the discovery and weakens my reason for leaving him out. Friedman's claim rests mainly on the tax-record mobility measurement and atlas work. I keep Friedman because the shortlisted discovery is defined by measurement with administrative data, and the cap forces a choice. I now see this as a close and contestable call. Third, a committee could reasonably judge the contribution to be primarily measurement, not a conceptual discovery, or prefer to wait. Those who prefer waiting have a coherent position.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B002 first and regards the omission of Katz as a real cost. She would not object to a configuration crediting him. She also objects that Friedman's role is not only data construction, since the data work is bound up with the design choices that make the estimates interpretable.
responses.response: You are right on both points, and your reply made me recheck my round-1 attribution. I described Friedman as the data-construction lead, which understates how the measurement and the interpretation are linked. I also assigned the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis to the wrong group. As far as I recall it was Chetty, Hendren and Katz, and that makes the Katz case stronger than I allowed. I still keep the trio, for a specific reason. The shortlisted discovery is mobility measured with population administrative data, and the atlas and mobility-measurement papers are where Friedman is central. A Chetty-Hendren-Katz variant would tilt the discovery toward the experimental exposure strand. If the committee wants that tilt, the clean test is which of the three it displaces. I would answer that Friedman is displaced on the exposure strand and Katz on the measurement strand. That shows the cap is making a real choice here, and the citation should be written so that it does not pretend otherwise.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B015 first and B002 seventh in his opening. He worries that B002 may prove data-driven rather than foundational. He argues that the diffuse credit in B015 and the concentration problem in B002 are mirror-image attribution difficulties, and he asks that his closeness to me as a co-author be weighed.
responses.response: I accept the mirror-image framing. I would add that the two problems differ in how a citation can handle them. In B015 the cap excludes five people with strong claims. In B002 the cap forces a choice among four, and a citation limited to measurement and exposure designs can state what is being credited. On data-driven versus foundational, I concede that B002 is less conceptual than the building blocks you credit in B015. My claim is only that a measurement standard and identification designs that others now use are a durable contribution, and that this should not be dismissed as mere data access. As you and Hassler both noted, our co-authorship means that agreement or disagreement among the three of us is not independent evidence. I note that my ranking of B015 fourth reflects the attribution problem you accept as its main weakness.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B004 first with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He accepts a Kiyotaki-Moore pair as a defensible fallback. He names overlap with the 2022 prize, indirect aggregate evidence and the position of Gertler as the weak points. He placed B002 sixth mainly on maturity and the causal reading of neighbourhood effects.
responses.response: Your maturity point is my main reservation about B002, and I do not think the evidence yet closes it. Replication in non-US administrative data and longer follow-up of the exposure-effect estimates would settle most of it for me. Until then the citation should stay close to what is established. I rank B004 second for the reasons you give. On the chair's question about the pair, I would prefer Kiyotaki and Moore alone to a trio in which Gertler's credit cannot be separated from the 2022 prize and from his place on B015. I think you are right that the committee should make that choice on the attribution argument, not on a wish for a smaller prize. Where we differ is on how much the indirect aggregate evidence should count against B004. I weigh it somewhat more than you do, but not enough to put the pair below B002 by a wide margin.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B015 first and B004 second. He says he would not oppose B002 in a later year, and he places it behind B015 because B015 has decades of confirmation and B002 has not had the same test. He also notes that his own social-mobility work is adjacent to B002.
responses.response: I agree that B015 has the longer record, and my objection is to attribution, not to merit. A Calvo-Taylor-Woodford cut can be defended with an originators-versus-developers criterion, but I find the exclusion of Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler hard to justify as principled rather than convenient. On a later year, waiting is a legitimate judgement only if it is tied to specific evidence. I would name non-US replication of exposure effects and longer follow-up as that evidence, and I would not let the passage of time substitute for it. The score on maturity should also be stated separately from attribution, as the chair's question asks. On maturity alone, B015 clearly beats B002. I place B002 first by weighting identification quality and attribution tractability more heavily than you do. Because we are co-authors, that difference should not be counted as independent corroboration either way.

uncertainties: Whether replication of the exposure-effect estimates in non-US administrative data and longer follow-up will be enough to settle the maturity concern, and whether a citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs is sufficient without it.
Whether Katz should be one of the three names, now that I believe his role in the exposure-effects strand is larger than I credited in round 1, and which of the other three he would displace.
How to weigh the data-infrastructure contribution against the conceptual and causal contributions, and whether the committee will see B002 as measurement rather than discovery.

Whether a Kiyotaki-Moore pair on B004 is, on a maturity-heavy weighting, a better single-part configuration than B002. I rank B002 first by a narrow margin and a committee could reasonably reverse it.
Whether Chetty's separate tax work (B037, not shortlisted) should be considered alongside this credit.
My attribution claims on Moving to Opportunity and the atlas papers come from general knowledge. I have not independently verified them, citation counts or replication results.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows no co-authorship or institutional connection with Chetty, Hendren, Friedman or Katz, so nothing links me to B002. I have frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell (secretary) and with John Hassler (chair), who both prefer B015. Hassler disclosed a joint paper with me. Krusell asked that our closeness be weighed, and I have treated their views as non-independent of each other and of mine. I also have a long collaboration with Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li, none of whom is on the shortlisted entries I propose. My own work on growth and long-run labour supply is thematically adjacent to my alternative B024, but my profile lists no co-authorship with Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz. I have not tried to adjudicate any recusal question, and I treat these as disclosures only.
